hero.headline: European Union Fines Google $1 Billion for Competition Violations
hero.body:
The European Union imposed a 890 million euro fine on Google for violating competition rules under the bloc's Digital Markets Act. The penalty marks another significant regulatory action against the tech giant and addresses violations related to both its search engine and app store operations.

The European Commission, the EU's executive arm, determined that Google abused its market power in two distinct ways. First, Google gave priority to its own services such as shopping and hotel deals in search results, treating them more favorably than those of competing companies. Second, Google prevented app developers from directing consumers toward cheaper offers on websites or alternative app stores. The Commission split the fine accordingly, assigning 460 million euros for the search-related breach and 430 million euros for the app store violation.

The regulatory action comes as Google has already begun making changes to address these concerns. The company has started testing modifications to how it displays search results featuring its own services, including shopping and flight options. A senior EU official noted that these changes represent "substantial progress towards compliance" with the Commission's requirements.

Moving forward, Google must treat third-party services appearing in its search results in a "fair and non-discriminatory manner." The company must also allow app developers to make offers outside Google's app store and direct users toward alternative payment options. These measures are intended to create a more level playing field for competitors on Google's platforms.

A senior EU official stated that consumers will benefit directly from the decision, noting that search results will differ in Europe and Google will need to adapt its search engine going forward.

The fine reflects the EU's position as a global leader in technology regulation. The bloc has consistently challenged business practices it views as anticompetitive and has established itself through a series of antitrust actions against major American technology companies. Google has faced multiple penalties from European regulators over the past decade for various competition-related issues, making it one of the most heavily fined companies in EU antitrust history.

The timing of the fine drew attention due to broader trade tensions. The decision was issued just hours before temporary global tariffs against approximately 60 countries were set to expire. However, EU officials stated they had no advance knowledge of how the United States might react to the fine. One official emphasized that the EU had the "sovereign right" to regulate American technology companies within its own jurisdiction and that the timing was not connected to tariff concerns.

Google has the option to appeal the decision and can request interim measures, including a suspension of the penalty, through European courts. Any appeal process could take years to resolve.

cards.headline: US continues strikes on Iran as attacks spread across region
cards.body:
The United States is intensifying military operations against Iran as the broader conflict expands across the Middle East, with multiple countries now engaged in strikes targeting energy infrastructure and military assets.

Israel has struck at least five energy sites in and around Tehran, creating thick plumes of black smoke over the capital. Iran's oil distribution company reported that four employees were killed in the airstrikes. Explosions in nearby Karaj reverberated across the region, leaving areas covered in smoke and the smell of burning oil.

In response to the Israeli strikes on energy facilities, a spokesperson for Iran's Revolutionary Guards warned of severe economic consequences. "If you can tolerate oil at more than $200 per barrel, continue this game," the IRGC official said. The Guards threatened to attack oil facilities in neighboring countries if strikes on Iran's energy infrastructure continue, accusing the US and Israel of targeting civilians and fuel facilities.

The US has sought to calm energy markets by pledging not to target Iran's oil infrastructure. Energy Secretary Chris Wright told CNN that any disruptions to petroleum and gas supplies would be brief, lasting only a few weeks at worst. Iran produces approximately 4 percent of global oil, much of it exported to China.

Iran launched fresh waves of attacks across the Gulf region on Sunday, with ballistic missiles striking toward Israel and drones targeting Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Bahrain and Kuwait. Saudi Arabia intercepted 15 drones, while strikes in Bahrain caused material damage to a desalination plant. Two people were killed in Al-Kharj, Saudi Arabia, after a projectile hit a residential area, and 12 others were injured.

The US military reported that a service member died from injuries sustained during an Iranian attack on American troops in Saudi Arabia, bringing the US death toll from the conflict to seven. The Trump administration is seeking billions of dollars more from Congress for operations in the region, which Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth says have already cost $37.5 billion.

Meanwhile, Yemen's Houthi forces, backed by Iran, claimed responsibility for attacks on oil tankers in the Red Sea, one of the world's most critical shipping routes. The Houthis announced a maritime embargo against Saudi Arabia, raising concerns about disruptions to global energy markets and supply chains.

The escalating military actions coincided with significant political developments in Iran. The clerical body responsible for selecting Iran's supreme leader announced that Mojtaba Khamenei, the second son of the late supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, would be his successor. This marks the first time since the 1979 Islamic Revolution that Iran's supreme leadership has passed from father to son.

The sustained military campaign involving multiple countries and affecting critical global trade routes represents a significant expansion of regional hostilities with potential consequences for world economies.

cards.headline: Global Oil Prices Near $100 as Iran Conflict Disrupts Shipping
cards.body:
Oil prices climbed toward $100 per barrel as escalating conflict with Iran threatened shipping routes through critical Middle Eastern waterways. The Houthis claimed responsibility for attacks on two vessels in the Red Sea, while Iran reported a third ship caught fire near the Strait of Hormuz.

The disruptions have pushed Brent crude past $98 per barrel, approaching the $100 threshold not seen since the initial surge following Russia's invasion of Ukraine. The Strait of Hormuz, which connects the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman, serves as a passage for roughly one-fifth of global oil supplies. Any sustained closure or disruption to shipping through the strait has immediate effects on energy markets worldwide.

The attacks represent an expansion of hostilities in the region. Houthi forces, backed by Iran, have previously targeted commercial shipping in the Red Sea as part of broader regional tensions. The reported fire near the Strait of Hormuz adds another flashpoint to an already volatile situation. Multiple vessels have now been affected across two key waterways that serve as vital arteries for global energy transport.

Rising oil prices carry immediate consequences for consumers and businesses. Transportation costs increase as fuel becomes more expensive, with those increases typically passed through to goods and services. The energy sector often serves as an early indicator of broader economic pressure, as sustained high oil prices can slow economic growth while accelerating inflation.

Markets are now watching whether prices will breach the $100 barrier and how long disruptions to shipping might continue. The situation remains fluid as Iran and the United States exchange threats and military posturing continues in the region. Energy traders are pricing in risk premiums as uncertainty about safe passage through these strategic waterways persists.

cards.headline: US signs nuclear cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia
cards.teaser: The US Department of Energy announced a nuclear energy cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia, saying it will give American firms access to the Saudi nuclear program.
cards.body:
The United States and Saudi Arabia have signed a nuclear cooperation agreement that includes both a peaceful nuclear cooperation deal and a bilateral safeguards agreement. US Department of Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Saudi Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman signed the accord, which will give American firms access to Saudi Arabia's nuclear energy programme.

The agreement could potentially allow Saudi Arabia to enrich uranium domestically in the future. Saudi Arabia, the world's largest crude oil exporter, is pursuing nuclear energy to diversify its power sources and free up more oil for international sales. The deal has sparked concerns in Europe, Asia, and the Middle East, where countries are seeking nuclear capabilities as a counterbalance to aggressive neighbors and perceived reduced American engagement.

cards.headline: Trump tariffs draw criticism from voters and international partners
cards.teaser: New tariff policies have generated opposition domestically and strained relationships with US allies.
cards.body:
President Trump's recently announced tariffs have sparked negative reactions from American voters and allied nations. The trade measures include a 50 percent tariff on Canadian goods, prompting concerns about consumer prices and economic impacts.

Analysts have examined how the tariffs could affect various sectors of the economy and consumer spending. The policies have created tension with trading partners, particularly Canada, as the administration pursues its trade agenda.

cards.headline: Diesel Shortage Threatens Farmers Worldwide as Strait of Hormuz Closes
cards.teaser: Limited diesel shipments are depriving farmers of fuel for irrigation pumps and threatening food supplies.
cards.body:
The closure of the Strait of Hormuz has restricted diesel shipments, creating fuel shortages that threaten agricultural production in multiple countries. Farmers rely on diesel to power irrigation pumps and other essential farm equipment, and the supply disruption has left many without adequate fuel during critical growing seasons.

The diesel crisis disproportionately affects poorer farming communities that lack alternative energy sources or financial reserves to absorb sharp price increases. The fuel shortage comes at a time when many regions depend on irrigation to maintain crop yields, raising concerns about food security in countries already facing economic pressures.

cards.headline: Senate Republicans question Trump administration on Iran military strategy
cards.teaser: Senate Republicans expressed concern over what they described as an unclear plan to end the ongoing military conflict with Iran, warning that rising casualties .
cards.body:
Senate Republicans expressed concern after a hearing with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday, saying they lack clarity on how the Iran conflict will end. The military engagement has resulted in increasing U.S. casualties, and Hegseth is requesting billions from Congress to help cover the rising costs of the war.

GOP lawmakers are worried about the political implications as midterm elections approach. Rising casualties and elevated gas prices linked to Middle East instability create economic and national security challenges for voters, putting pressure on Senate Republicans defending their majority.

cards.headline: Ebola spreads in crowded displacement camps in Congo
cards.teaser: The Ebola virus is spreading through camps housing one million people displaced by violence in Congo, where residents face dangerous conditions and limited access to clean water.
cards.body:
An Ebola outbreak is affecting displacement camps in the Democratic Republic of the Congo that house approximately one million people who fled violence. The camps are situated in the epicenter of the outbreak, with residents facing severe hardship as they attempt to contain the virus with minimal access to clean water.

The crowded and unsanitary conditions in the camps create ideal circumstances for rapid disease transmission. Health workers treating Ebola patients in the DRC have faced significant risk, with at least one humanitarian worker requiring medical evacuation and specialist monitoring in the United Kingdom following potential exposure to the virus.

cards.headline: Russian military intelligence officer flees Japan after exposure
cards.teaser: A Russian military intelligence officer left Japan after being identified as conducting espionage operations from an Aeroflot airline office in Tokyo.
cards.body:
A Russian military intelligence officer fled Japan following a New York Times report exposing his espionage activities. The officer had been operating under cover at the Aeroflot airline office in Tokyo, using the commercial entity as a base for intelligence operations.

The officer's departure came shortly after the Times publication revealed his activities to the public. The incident demonstrates how intelligence services leverage legitimate businesses as fronts for covert operations in foreign countries.

cards.headline: Ukraine strikes Russian commercial warehouses in escalating air campaign
cards.teaser: Ukraine expanded its long-range attacks to target commercial warehouses in Russia, aiming to bring the war closer to ordinary Russian citizens.
cards.body:
Ukraine has begun striking commercial warehouses in Russia as part of an escalating air campaign. The targets include facilities operated by Russia's equivalent of Amazon and other commercial distribution centers.

Kyiv stated the strategy aims to bring the conflict closer to home for ordinary Russians by disrupting civilian commerce and logistics. The shift represents an expansion of Ukraine's long-range strike capabilities beyond purely military targets.

cards.headline: Indian police crack down on youth protest movement in capital
cards.teaser: Police in India moved to suppress a protest movement known as the 'Cockroaches' as demonstrators held a sit-in in the capital demanding education reforms.
cards.body:
Indian police cracked down on demonstrators participating in a youth-led sit-in protest in New Delhi. The movement, known as the 'Cockroaches,' is composed largely of Generation Z activists pushing for improvements to the education system.

Following the police action, protesters turned to social media, creating memes and reels to document their experiences. These posts became a way for young demonstrators to process what happened and maintain momentum for their cause despite the crackdown.

cards.headline: Third firefighter dies battling European wildfires
cards.teaser: A third firefighter has died fighting wildfires across Europe as thousands of people were evacuated from affected areas in France.
cards.body:
A firefighter became the third to die while battling ongoing wildfires across Europe. The death occurred as fires continue to spread through multiple countries on the continent.

France evacuated thousands of people from areas threatened by the blazes. The wildfires have stretched firefighting resources across Europe as crews work to contain multiple active fire zones.

hero.headline: White House cuts nutrition education program while promoting healthy eating agenda
hero.body:
The Trump administration is pursuing nutrition education through medical schools even as it eliminated SNAP-Ed, a federal program that provided dietary guidance to low-income Americans. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. unveiled the medical school initiative this week, creating a stark contrast with the earlier decision to cut the community-based nutrition program.

Kennedy announced that 53 medical schools have voluntarily committed to a new nutrition education effort. Starting in autumn 2026, these institutions will provide 40 hours of nutrition education or its equivalent to medical students. Kennedy described the initiative as central to implementing the Make America Healthy Again agenda.

"This is how we implement the MAHA agenda," Kennedy said at the announcement event, calling it "a transformative breakthrough in medical education that will reshape the way we train doctors in our country."

The medical schools participating in the program must evaluate their current nutrition instruction levels, designate a faculty member to oversee nutrition education, and publish information about how they will meet the 40-hour requirement. Institutions span both Republican and Democratic-leaning states, including the University of Alabama at Birmingham, University of Florida, George Washington University, New York University, and Tufts University.

Several highly ranked universities declined to participate despite having respected medical schools. Brown University, Columbia University, and Cornell University chose not to join, even though they had previously reached funding-related agreements with the Trump administration.

Kennedy has also signaled broader intentions regarding food safety. Last week, he suggested the administration may seek to remove certain foods from the market if companies cannot demonstrate their safety. He specifically mentioned major coffee chains, stating the administration would ask them to provide safety data for high-sugar beverages marketed to teenagers.

The medical school initiative contrasts with the administration's elimination of SNAP-Ed, which provided nutrition education to millions of low-income Americans through community organizations, health departments, and educational institutions. The program offered cooking demonstrations, nutrition workshops, and educational materials to families receiving Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits.

Many doctors and researchers have previously criticized Kennedy's positions, particularly regarding vaccines, as lacking scientific grounding. Health experts have noted that nutrition education represents a cost-effective intervention that can reduce long-term healthcare costs associated with diet-related chronic diseases.

The medical school push reflects a broader effort by the Trump administration to promote its priorities within American higher education, marking a departure from the country's traditional emphasis on academic independence. Kennedy's nutrition education initiative has managed to attract medical schools across diverse political landscapes, even as questions remain about how the medical focus aligns with the elimination of community-level nutrition assistance programs.

cards.headline: Law enforcement experts raise concerns about ICE vetting after fatal shootings
cards.teaser: Recent deadly shootings by ICE officers have prompted questions about hiring practices during a period of rapid agency expansion.
cards.body:
Fatal shootings by Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers in Texas and Maine have prompted law enforcement experts to scrutinize the agency's vetting procedures. The incidents occurred during a period of rapid expansion, when ICE significantly increased its workforce through accelerated hiring.

Police experts worry that swift hiring campaigns can pressure agencies to reduce screening rigor for new officers. The shootings have raised questions about whether ICE maintained adequate vetting standards while prioritizing speed to meet staffing needs.

cards.headline: Bipartisan housing bill becomes law
cards.teaser: Congress passed and the president signed legislation aimed at addressing housing affordability, though implementation challenges lie ahead.
cards.body:
A housing bill that received support from both parties has been signed into law. The legislation includes provisions to address housing affordability and disaster recovery funding mechanisms, marking a rare area of bipartisan cooperation in Congress.

The new law will affect housing policy across states, with specific changes to how disaster recovery funds are allocated and distributed. Implementation of the bill's provisions now falls to federal agencies and state governments, which will determine how the measures translate into practical changes for housing markets and disaster-affected communities.

cards.headline: FDA panel reviews proposal to ease peptide access
cards.teaser: Food and Drug Administration advisers are examining evidence for seven peptides that could become more widely available.
cards.body:
A Food and Drug Administration advisory panel is evaluating seven peptides to determine whether current restrictions should be relaxed. The panel is assessing scientific evidence on the compounds' safety and efficacy.

If the advisers vote favorably, the peptides could become more accessible to the public. While the FDA typically adopts its advisory committees' recommendations, the agency retains final decision-making authority.

cards.headline: Redistricting changes divide predominantly Black areas across six states
cards.teaser: New congressional district maps have split up largely Black communities in Republican-controlled states.
cards.body:
Maps reveal how redistricting efforts initiated by President Trump have disproportionately affected predominantly Black congressional districts in six states controlled by Republican legislatures. The new district boundaries have altered the geographic composition of areas with significant Black populations.

This redistricting battle has drawn attention to how congressional maps shape representation and voting power in communities of color, particularly in Republican-led states where the remapping process has taken place.

cards.headline: Catholic sisters plan new order to support clergy abuse survivors
cards.teaser: Two women are establishing a religious community dedicated to helping victims of abuse within the Catholic Church.
cards.body:
Sisters Theresa Alethia and Danielle Lussier are establishing the Sisters of the Little Way of Beauty, Truth and Goodness, a new Catholic religious order dedicated to helping survivors of clergy sexual abuse. The sisters aim to create a community centered on supporting and accompanying those harmed by abuse.

Their initiative represents a distinctive focus within Catholic religious life, directly responding to the ongoing clergy abuse crisis and its lasting effects on survivors.

cards.headline: US signs nuclear cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia
cards.teaser: The Department of Energy announced a deal that will give American companies access to Saudi Arabia's nuclear energy program.
cards.body:
The United States and Saudi Arabia have signed a nuclear cooperation agreement aimed at peaceful energy development. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman signed both a "peaceful nuclear cooperation agreement" and a "bilateral safeguards agreement." The US Department of Energy stated the deal will give American firms greater access to Saudi Arabia's nuclear energy program.

The agreement comes as the Trump administration seeks to expand nuclear partnerships in the region. The deal could potentially allow Saudi Arabia to pursue uranium enrichment in the future as part of its energy infrastructure development.

cards.headline: European Union Fines Google $1 Billion Over Search Practices
cards.teaser: The EU accused Google of anti-competitive business practices in a decision that adds strain to trans-Atlantic trade relations.
cards.body:
The European Commission fined Google's parent company Alphabet €890 million ($1 billion) for violating the Digital Markets Act. Google prioritized its own services, such as shopping and hotel deals, over rival offerings in search results, breaching EU competition rules.

The penalty also addresses a second violation involving Google's Android app store, where the company blocked developers from directing users to alternative payment options. The EU required Google to treat third-party services appearing in its results fairly and without discrimination.

cards.headline: Alphabet Stock Drops Despite Strong Earnings Report
cards.teaser: Google's parent company reported revenue that exceeded expectations, but shares fell on news of increased capital spending for 2026.
cards.body:
Alphabet reported second-quarter earnings that beat analyst projections, but the company's stock declined as investors reacted to planned increases in capital expenditures. The Google parent company announced higher spending plans for 2026, focusing on infrastructure and technology investments that will affect near-term profitability.

Google Cloud has emerged as a significant profit driver for Alphabet, contributing to the strong revenue performance. The company has shifted resources toward cloud computing and artificial intelligence, areas that require substantial upfront investment but promise long-term growth as businesses continue migrating operations to cloud platforms.

cards.headline: Nestlé Sells Half of Water Business to Platinum Equity for $3.4 Billion
cards.teaser: The deal creates a joint venture valued at roughly $5.6 billion for Nestlé's water and premium beverage brands.
cards.body:
Nestlé agreed to sell a 50 percent stake in its water division to private equity firm Platinum Equity in a transaction valuing the business at approximately $5.6 billion. The deal structures the water unit as a joint venture called Peranel, which will include brands such as Perrier and other bottled water products.

The sale allows Nestlé to reduce its exposure to the bottled water category while maintaining a stake in the business. The food and beverage company has been reshaping its portfolio to focus on higher-growth categories, with coffee emerging as a key driver of revenue growth in recent quarters.

cards.headline: Westinghouse Positioned to Benefit From Nuclear Energy Revival
cards.teaser: The company that filed for bankruptcy in 2017 stands to gain from growing support for nuclear power.
cards.body:
Westinghouse Electric Company is positioned to benefit from renewed interest in nuclear energy, seven years after filing for bankruptcy protection. Growing support for nuclear power as a low-carbon energy source has created new opportunities for the nuclear reactor manufacturer and service provider.

President Trump's deal with Saudi Arabia includes nuclear energy components that could generate business for Westinghouse. The agreement represents part of a broader shift in energy policy that views nuclear power as essential to meeting electricity demand while reducing carbon emissions, reversing decades of declining investment in the nuclear industry.

cards.headline: Salad Chain Sales Drop After Taylor Farms Recall
cards.teaser: Chains including Chopt and Chipotle saw foot traffic decline following a produce recall and shifting guidance from regulators.
cards.body:
Restaurant chains that specialize in salads experienced declining customer traffic after Taylor Farms issued a recall and the FDA provided changing messages about food safety. Chopt and Chipotle were among the chains affected by consumer concerns about cyclosporiasis, a parasitic infection linked to contaminated produce.

The recall and subsequent confusion about which products were safe created uncertainty for both restaurants and consumers. Fast-casual chains that built their businesses around fresh produce and salad offerings have seen sales affected as customers avoid items they perceive as risky until the situation clarifies.

cards.headline: Samsung Launches New Foldable Phones Ahead of Expected Apple Entry
cards.teaser: Samsung unveiled its latest Galaxy Z Fold and Flip models as the foldable phone market prepares for competition from Apple.
cards.body:
Samsung introduced its new Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra, Fold8, and Flip8 foldable smartphones, describing them as refined devices designed for different user needs. The company positioned the launch as an overhaul of its foldable phone lineup, with changes to design and features across the product range.

The release comes as Apple is expected to enter the foldable phone market for the first time. Samsung raised prices on its new models despite the anticipated competition. The company has dominated the foldable phone segment since pioneering the category and is working to maintain its position as other manufacturers prepare similar devices.

cards.headline: Apple Plans Major Updates to MacBook and iMac Product Lines
cards.teaser: Reports detail Apple's development roadmap for Mac computers over the next two years, including new processors and design changes.
cards.body:
Apple is preparing significant updates to its MacBook and iMac computers to meet demand related to artificial intelligence capabilities. The company's plans include new M6 processors for the Mac Mini and A19 Pro chips for a device referred to as the MacBook Neo. Reports suggest the updates go beyond previously rumored touchscreen additions.

The MacBook Neo 2 is among the products in development, though specific details about features and release timing remain limited. The refresh of Apple's Mac lineup represents an effort to equip its computers with hardware capable of handling AI workloads. The roadmap covers products expected to launch over approximately the next two years.

cards.headline: ServiceNow Invests $40 Million in Indian Banking Software Company
cards.teaser: The enterprise software firm is backing BusinessNext as it expands its financial services offerings globally.
cards.body:
ServiceNow has invested $40 million in BusinessNext, an Indian banking software company. The investment strengthens ServiceNow's position in financial services technology and provides BusinessNext with a strategic partner to expand globally.

Through this partnership, BusinessNext gains access to resources and market reach to scale its AI-powered banking software beyond India. ServiceNow, in turn, acquires banking-specific technology expertise as part of its broader expansion into the financial services sector.

cards.headline: IBM Attributes Mainframe Sales Decline to AI Budget Shifts
cards.teaser: After a sharp stock drop, IBM's CEO said corporate spending on AI disrupted traditional hardware budgets.
cards.body:
IBM's stock price fell sharply after the company warned of weak mainframe sales. The CEO attributed the decline to corporate budget shifts toward artificial intelligence investments, characterizing the impact as temporary rather than a fundamental threat to the mainframe business.

The company maintained that AI is not making mainframe computers obsolete, but rather that customer spending priorities have temporarily shifted away from mainframe purchases as organizations redirect hardware budgets toward AI initiatives.

cards.headline: Researchers Document Vector-Based Navigation in Fruit Flies
cards.teaser: A study published in Nature describes how Drosophila use a vector strategy for navigating by smell.
cards.body:
Scientists have identified how fruit flies navigate using scent, publishing their findings in the journal Nature. The research reveals that Drosophila employ a vector-based strategy for olfactory navigation, using directional information from odors to move through their environment.

The study provides new understanding of how insects process smell to guide movement. Vector-based navigation means the flies calculate direction and distance based on scent gradients rather than simply moving toward stronger smells. The research contributes to broader scientific knowledge about how sensory information translates into navigation behavior in animals.

cards.headline: Researchers Observe Orcas Ramming Ocean Sunfish
cards.teaser: Scientists documented orcas working together to strike sunfish with enough force to cause the fish to burst.
cards.body:
Marine scientists have documented orcas engaging in a striking hunting technique: ramming giant sunfish with such force that the prey breaks into pieces. In observed instances, one orca would hold the sunfish in its jaws while a second whale charged at high speed, shattering the fish into thousands of fragments.

Since the sunfish were already dead when the ramming occurred, researchers suggest the behavior may serve as entertainment or play rather than purely for feeding. The activity could also help younger orcas learn to access food more efficiently. Scientists continue investigating why orcas employ this dramatic technique.

hero.headline: Newcastle agree £34 million deal for Monaco midfielder Aladji Bamba
hero.body:
Newcastle United has reached an agreement to sign midfielder Aladji Bamba from AS Monaco for £34 million. The player is scheduled to arrive on Thursday to complete a medical examination and sign a long-term contract with the Premier League club.

The transfer represents a significant investment by Newcastle as they continue to strengthen their squad. Bamba, who has been playing in France's top division with Monaco, will add depth to Newcastle's midfield options once the deal is finalized.

The signing follows a period of increased spending by Newcastle since new ownership took control of the club. The club has targeted players from top European leagues as part of their strategy to compete at the highest levels of English and European football.

Bamba's arrival is subject to him passing the required medical tests and agreeing personal terms, though both are expected to be formalities given that he is traveling to complete the transfer. The long-term contract indicates Newcastle's commitment to building around the midfielder as part of their squad plans.

Once the medical and contract signing are complete, Bamba will join Newcastle's squad for the remainder of the season. The transfer fee places him among the more expensive signings in the club's recent transfer activity, reflecting both his potential and the competitive nature of the current transfer market for midfield talent.

This move comes as Newcastle continues to reshape their playing squad under their current management structure. The club has been active in the transfer market, seeking to reinforce key areas of their team to improve their performance in the Premier League and European competitions.

The addition of Bamba represents Newcastle's attempt to bolster their midfield depth and creativity. With the midfielder arriving from a top European league, he brings experience and quality that should help Newcastle's ambitions in the second half of the season.

Newcastle's recruitment strategy has focused on acquiring players from established leagues who have proven themselves at a high level. Bamba fits this profile, having established himself as a regular fixture in Monaco's midfield setup.

The club's willingness to invest significantly in midfield reinforcement underscores their determination to compete with the leading sides in English football. The £34 million outlay demonstrates their commitment to bringing in quality players who can make an immediate impact.

Staff at Newcastle will be hoping that Bamba's arrival provides the boost needed to challenge for a strong finish to the season. His technical abilities and experience should provide options for the manager in terms of tactical flexibility and squad rotation.

The transfer window activity reflects Newcastle's broader ambitions as they look to establish themselves as genuine contenders in the Premier League. With Bamba's addition to the squad, Newcastle continues to build towards their long-term objectives.

cards.headline: St Helens head coach Paul Rowley leaves club
cards.teaser: Paul Rowley has departed St Helens with immediate effect, less than a year after taking the Super League head coach position.
cards.body:
St Helens head coach Paul Rowley has left the Super League club with immediate effect, less than a year into his role. The departure comes just one day before the club's scheduled derby match.

The timing of Rowley's exit means St Helens must arrange interim coaching cover for the upcoming fixture and reassess their coaching structure going forward.

cards.headline: England's 2027 Ashes schedule excludes northern venues
cards.teaser: Neither Old Trafford nor Headingley will host a men's Ashes Test match when England faces Australia next summer.
cards.body:
Neither Old Trafford in Manchester nor Headingley in Leeds will host men's Ashes Test matches during England's series against Australia next summer. Both grounds are traditional venues for the rivalry.

The scheduling decision means no Test matches from the 2027 Ashes will take place in the north of England.

cards.headline: Martin Kaymer expresses doubt about LIV Golf's future
cards.teaser: Golfer Martin Kaymer said it is highly unlikely the 2026 LIV Golf team championship will take place and questioned the circuit's future.
cards.body:
Professional golfer Martin Kaymer has cast doubt on LIV Golf's future, stating that the circuit's 2026 team championship is "highly unlikely" to take place. According to Kaymer, even the organization's CEO lacks clarity about the direction of the breakaway league.

Kaymer's comments reveal internal uncertainty within LIV Golf regarding its operations and long-term plans. The circuit has faced ongoing scrutiny about its structure and sustainability since launching as an alternative to traditional professional golf.

cards.headline: Spanish footballers receive tomatoes after World Cup victory
cards.teaser: Spain's Fabian Ruiz and Gavi were each given their body weight in tomatoes upon returning to their hometown following the World Cup win.
cards.body:
Spanish midfielders Fabian Ruiz and Gavi received an unusual homecoming gift upon returning to their hometown of Los Palacios y Villafranca. Each player was presented with 150 kilograms of tomatoes, matching their respective body weights.

The quirky tribute celebrated the players' contributions to Spain's World Cup campaign. The reward reflected local traditions in the Andalusian town, where both footballers grew up.

cards.headline: Former UFC champion Jessica Andrade works as delivery driver during injury recovery
cards.teaser: Ex-UFC champion Jessica Andrade has taken a job as a delivery driver while recovering from injury to support herself financially.
cards.body:
Jessica Andrade, a former UFC champion, has taken on work as a delivery driver while recovering from injury. She stated she will do "whatever it takes" to earn a living during this period away from competition.

The situation underscores the financial pressures fighters face when unable to compete and earn fight purses due to injuries.

cards.headline: Caitlin Clark receives seventh technical foul, nears suspension
cards.teaser: Indiana Fever guard Caitlin Clark was assessed her seventh technical foul of the season, putting her one away from a one-game suspension.
cards.body:
Caitlin Clark received her seventh technical foul during a game in which the Indiana Fever scored a franchise-record 123 points against the Connecticut Sun. The technical foul puts Clark one away from triggering an automatic one-game suspension under league rules.

Clark received the technical after what was described as a scoreboard taunt during the victory. The Fever's offensive output set a new team record, but Clark's accumulation of technical fouls has become a concern as she approaches the threshold that would force her to miss a game.

hero.headline: Venice Film Festival Announces 2026 Lineup With New Films From McDonagh, Zeller, and Boyle
hero.body:
The Venice Film Festival has revealed its 2026 lineup, showcasing new works from prominent international directors including Martin McDonagh, Florian Zeller, Danny Boyle, Werner Herzog, Lance Oppenheim, Nanni Moretti, and Hirokazu Kore-eda. The festival will also debut a documentary about the Oasis reunion, blending acclaimed cinema with mainstream entertainment at the prestigious Italian event.

The 82nd edition runs from August 14 to 21 and features 21 world premieres, six international premieres, one European premiere, and 23 regional premieres across its competition sections. Robert Pattinson will star in a film titled Primetime, while McDonagh will present Wild Horse Nine.

One significant entry in the Horizons competition is "The Difficult Bride," a supernatural feminist drama directed by Rubaiyat Hossain. The film marks a historic milestone as the first Bangladeshi feature film to screen at Venice. The cast features three Bangladesh National Film Award winners: Azmeri Haque Badhon, Rikita Nondine Shimu, and Sunerah Kamal. Films Boutique has secured international sales rights for the project.

Another Horizons selection, "Oasis" by writer-director Jannis Lenz, has been picked up by Totem for international sales ahead of its Venice premiere. The film is centered on a school setting where a viral video triggers a narrative exploring themes of fear, exclusion, and violence. Totem added the film to its sales slate as the company transitions its primary focus toward production.

The Sarajevo Film Festival, which specializes in South-East European cinema, simultaneously announced its competition programs during the same period. The festival revealed lineups across four competition sections, featuring 21 world premieres, six international premieres, one European premiere, and 23 regional premieres. The Sarajevo festival will run from August 14 to 21, with nine narrative features from South-East European filmmakers competing in the main section.

This year's Venice lineup represents a diverse range of storytelling approaches. Beyond the major names attached to various projects, the festival continues its tradition of discovering emerging voices and supporting cinema from underrepresented regions. The inclusion of "The Difficult Bride" demonstrates Venice's commitment to expanding global representation in its programming, particularly in highlighting cinema from South Asian countries.

The parallel timing of Venice and Sarajevo festivals underscores the importance of late summer as a significant period for festival cinema. These events serve as launching pads for films that will compete throughout the upcoming awards season and establish themselves within the international film market. The combination of established filmmakers and fresh talent announced for Venice's 2026 edition suggests another compelling year for the festival.

cards.headline: Tom Holland to Play Fred Astaire in Upcoming Biopic, Plans to Perform All Dance Sequences
cards.teaser: Tom Holland will portray Fred Astaire in a biopic and intends to perform all the dancing himself.
cards.body:
Tom Holland announced he will play Fred Astaire in an upcoming biopic and plans to handle all the dancing himself. The actor is currently promoting two consecutive blockbuster films, The Odyssey and Spider-Man: Brand New Day, but is already preparing for the role of the celebrated dancer.

Holland acknowledged the physical demands of portraying Astaire, stating he has significant preparation ahead. The project represents a departure from his recent action-oriented roles, focusing instead on the grace and technical skill required to embody one of Hollywood's most iconic dancers.

cards.headline: Whoopi Goldberg Defends Elliot Page's Casting in The Odyssey Against Conservative Critics
cards.teaser: Whoopi Goldberg responded to conservative criticism of Elliot Page's casting in Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey.
cards.body:
Whoopi Goldberg addressed criticism of Elliot Page's casting in Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey during an episode of The View. She dismissed a clip of commentator Ben Shapiro, who called the casting choice a mistake and referenced Page's physical stature, describing him as about 5'2" and 105 pounds.

Goldberg questioned why critics were concerned about the casting decision, suggesting those opposed to it simply avoid seeing the film. Her remarks came as part of a broader pushback against conservative commentators who have criticized the transgender actor's role in the upcoming film.

cards.headline: Comcast Reports Second Quarter Gains From World Cup and Peacock Profitability
cards.teaser: Comcast's second quarter was boosted by World Cup broadcasts and Peacock streaming achieving profitability for the first time.
cards.body:
Comcast reported strong second-quarter performance driven by World Cup coverage on its Telemundo Spanish-language network and improved results from Peacock, its streaming service, which turned profitable for the first time.

The streaming milestone represents a significant achievement after years of investment. However, the company's cable and broadband divisions faced headwinds that offset some of these gains during the period.

cards.headline: Jason Alexander Apologizes to Courtney Stodden for Sketch Filmed When She Was 17
cards.teaser: The Seinfeld actor issued an apology to the reality star for what he described as an inappropriate Funny Or Die sketch.
cards.body:
Jason Alexander has apologized to Courtney Stodden for appearing in a Funny Or Die sketch with her when she was 17 years old. The Seinfeld actor said he "truly regrets" his participation in the video.

The apology addresses the sketch, which has faced renewed scrutiny in recent years for its appropriateness given Stodden's age at the time of filming.

cards.headline: Isabel Davis Appointed Director of BFI National Lottery Filmmaking Fund
cards.teaser: The British Film Institute named Isabel Davis to oversee approximately $26.8 million in annual funding for independent filmmakers.
cards.body:
Isabel Davis has been appointed director of the BFI National Lottery Filmmaking Funds, where she will oversee approximately 20 million pounds ($26.8 million) in annual support for U.K. independent filmmakers. Davis joins the British Film Institute from Screen Scotland, where she served as executive director for eight years.

Davis begins a five-year fixed-term contract in the role. Her appointment places her at the helm of one of the U.K.'s primary funding mechanisms for independent film production, with responsibility for distributing lottery proceeds to filmmakers across the country.

cards.headline: Daniel Wu Receives Best From the East Award at New York Asian Film Festival
cards.teaser: The actor was honored at the festival during a period that has seen him return to Hong Kong's two biggest film franchises.
cards.body:
Daniel Wu received the Best from the East Award at the New York Asian Film Festival, recognizing his contributions to Asian cinema. The honor comes as Wu has returned to starring roles in Hong Kong's two biggest franchises: Cold War 1994 and the Twilight of the Warriors series.

Cold War 1994 is the third installment in the Cold War series. Wu's recent work has placed him at the center of major Hong Kong film productions, marking a homecoming for the actor who has worked across international markets throughout his career.

hero.headline: Trump administration signs nuclear cooperation deal with Saudi Arabia
hero.teaser: The agreement could eventually permit Saudi Arabia to enrich uranium, drawing criticism from nonproliferation experts and Israel supporters.
hero.body:
The Trump administration has signed a nuclear cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia that could eventually permit the kingdom to enrich uranium domestically. The deal immediately generated criticism from nonproliferation advocates and Israel supporters who worry the technology could enable Saudi Arabia to develop nuclear weapons.

The agreement represents a notable shift in U.S. nuclear policy toward Saudi Arabia. The U.S. Department of Energy announced that Secretary Chris Wright and Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman signed a "peaceful nuclear cooperation agreement" along with a "bilateral safeguards agreement." Under the deal, American companies will receive priority access to supply nuclear reactors and fuel to Saudi Arabia. The arrangement is expected to last for decades and could be worth billions of dollars to the U.S. nuclear industry.

The accord drew swift backlash from multiple quarters. Critics have highlighted the stark contrast between the administration's approach to Saudi Arabia and its stance on Iran. The U.S. is currently engaged in military conflict with Iran partly over uranium enrichment concerns, yet the Saudi deal explicitly permits the kingdom to potentially pursue enrichment activities after a joint study period.

Nonproliferation experts have expressed particular concern about safeguards in the agreement. The deal reportedly allows the Saudis to bar international inspectors from certain nuclear sites, which analysts warn could leave little oversight preventing a civilian nuclear program from becoming a covert weapons operation. Saudi Arabia, like Iran, is a signatory to the nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty. The Saudi crown prince has previously stated his country would develop nuclear weapons if Iran did so.

Observers have noted the agreement is less stringent than a 2009 nuclear cooperation deal negotiated with the United Arab Emirates, another Gulf state. Some analysts suggest financial considerations may have influenced the administration's approach, as sales of nuclear reactors to Saudi Arabia could generate substantial revenue for American firms.

The timing of the announcement also proved controversial. It comes as the Trump administration seeks congressional funding for its ongoing military operations in the Middle East. Defense officials have requested billions in additional appropriations to sustain the campaign.

One notable element of the agreement is its separation from previous diplomatic conditions. An earlier version of a potential Saudi nuclear deal had been tied to Saudi Arabia normalizing relations with Israel. That requirement has now been dropped, with Saudi officials stating that recognition of Israel remains contingent on establishing "a credible and irreversible path to a Palestinian state."

House Democrats have called for congressional hearings on the agreement, signaling likely legislative scrutiny of the administration's approach to nuclear cooperation in the Middle East.

cards.headline: Senate Republicans question Trump administration on Iran military strategy
cards.teaser: Senate Republicans expressed concern over what they described as an unclear plan to end the ongoing military conflict with Iran, warning that rising casualties .
cards.body:
Senate Republicans expressed concern after a hearing with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday, saying they lack clarity on how the Iran conflict will end. The military engagement has resulted in increasing U.S. casualties, and Hegseth is requesting billions from Congress to help cover the rising costs of the war.

GOP lawmakers are worried about the political implications as midterm elections approach. Rising casualties and elevated gas prices linked to Middle East instability create economic and national security challenges for voters, putting pressure on Senate Republicans defending their majority.

cards.headline: GOP senators criticize Trump Media plan to sell early access to president's posts
cards.teaser: Republican lawmakers opposing President Trump objected to a proposal that would give trading firms advance access to market-moving social media posts.
cards.body:
Republican senators opposing President Trump have criticized a proposal by Trump Media Technology Group to sell faster access to his Truth Social posts to wealthy trading firms. The plan would give financial companies an advantage in markets by allowing them to see potentially market-moving presidential statements before the public, creating concerns about a two-tiered system where well-funded traders could profit from advance knowledge of communications that often influence financial markets.

Trump Media floated the arrangement as a potential revenue stream for the company, which operates the Truth Social platform.

cards.headline: House advances bill to shift data center costs away from electric ratepayers
cards.teaser: Bipartisan legislation gaining support would require states to consider standards that place infrastructure costs on tech companies rather than consumers.
cards.body:
A bipartisan bill seeking to protect electric ratepayers from data center costs is gaining momentum in the House amid growing backlash against sprawling AI infrastructure. The Ratepayer Protection Act would require states to consider standards that shift costs to tech companies rather than passing them on to consumers through higher electric bills.

Lawmakers are facing pressure to act as Americans express frustration over the impact of data centers on their utility bills. The legislation comes as tech companies rapidly expand AI infrastructure that demands massive amounts of electricity, raising concerns about who bears the financial burden of the buildout.

cards.headline: Democrats hold double-digit lead in congressional ballot polling
cards.teaser: A new Emerson College poll shows Democrats ahead of Republicans by 11 points as the midterm battle for House and Senate control intensifies.
cards.body:
Democrats lead Republicans by 11 points on a generic congressional ballot in a new national survey from Emerson College Polling. The poll found 53 percent of voters sided with the generic Democrat, up three points from the previous month, while 42 percent sided with Republicans.

The results come as the midterm fight for control of both the House and Senate intensifies. The double-digit Democratic advantage represents a significant shift in voter sentiment as both parties prepare for elections that will determine which party controls Congress.

cards.headline: Senate Democratic super PAC reserves $54 million for final midterm push
cards.teaser: Senate Majority PAC is targeting four Republican-held seats in advertising that reveals where Democrats see opportunities to flip control.
cards.body:
Senate Majority PAC, aligned with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, is booking another $54 million in television advertising for the final stretch of the midterm campaign. The reservations target four Republican-held seats, offering insight into where Democrats believe they can flip control.

The new advertising footprint contrasts with Republicans' recent major reservation, which focused largely on defending incumbents and protecting the GOP majority. The Democratic super PAC's strategy indicates the party sees viable paths to gaining seats currently held by Republicans as the midterm election approaches.

cards.headline: USAID elimination hampers federal response to cyclospora outbreak
cards.teaser: The Trump administration's dismantling of the international development agency last year affected funding for divisions responding to record infection numbers.
cards.body:
The Trump administration and the Department of Government Efficiency's elimination of the U.S. Agency for International Development last year continues to affect the federal response to a record number of cyclosporiasis infections. USAID had helped fund key divisions involved in responding to the parasitic disease outbreak.

The agency's dismantling set off consequences still being felt in what officials describe as a sluggish federal response to the elevated infection rates. The parasitic illness, caused by the cyclospora parasite, has reached record numbers as the government works to address the outbreak without the international development agency's support structure.
